#59665 [RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs
vllm-project/vllm#59665 · benchislett · OPEN · created 2026-10-01T18:53:37Z
[RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs
Motivation.
Frontier coding models have become extremely proficient at inference model optimization and efficient GPU kernel development. The frequency of new vLLM PRs is rapidly increasing, and is outpacing reviewer bandwidth.
Powered by fully autonomous optimization loops (e.g. “autoresearch”), optimization development can be scaled horizontally across a wide range of models, hardware architectures, and deployment scenarios.
The potential speedups are extremely large, but careful steps must be taken to ensure that vLLM’s code quality, usability, and reliability is not sacrificed in the process — this is why we have a comprehensive review process. Striking a balance between contribution barriers and performance upside is critical.
The fundamental goal of the fast-track is to merge PRs faster, with the same standard of quality. The way to achieve this is by systematically verifying aspects that ordinarily require manual reviewer verification (correctness, performance, no risk of breaking other workloads, etc.). By focusing on a subset of PRs whose changes are strictly contained to an isolated module (namely, the “model forward pass”) we can tailor guardrails to decrease reviewer involvement while maintaining a high bar for stability.
1. Proposed Change.
I propose a relaxation of the review and merge requirements, limited to cases where changes are contained, comprehensively validated, and provably limited to explicitly validated deployment scenarios.
The remainder of the RFC details the following:

Process changes we can make to more efficiently merge “safe” optimization PRs
How we can systematically ensure that an eligible PR is “safe to merge”

1.1: One-Touch Merge (“LGTM”)
Reviewers often need to revisit PRs multiple times throughout review: one pass to leave comments, another pass to approve and enable CI, additional passes to rerun/retry CI, and possibly a final force-merge request must be made.
For contained model optimizations, much of this can be prevented:

Process changes we can make to more efficiently merge “safe” optimization PRs
How we can systematically ensure that an eligible PR is “safe to merge”

1.1: One-Touch Merge (“LGTM”)
Reviewers often need to revisit PRs multiple times throughout review: one pass to leave comments, another pass to approve and enable CI, additional passes to rerun/retry CI, and possibly a final force-merge request must be made.
For contained model optimizations, much of this can be prevented:

If no comments are required, a single reviewer action approves the PR and starts an automated procedure to merge: CI runs and executes an automated procedure of rebase and retry until the PR goes in (up to 3 times) or a fallback force-merge is automatically requested.
If only trivial edits or conflict resolution are requested, a reviewer may submit a “conditional approval” on the requested changes. After the changes are made the automated merge procedure begins. The “conditional approval” persists through rebase, conflict resolution, acceptance of reviewer-suggested edits, and changes localized to tests/, provided the changes preserve the approved behavior. An amount of trust is delegated to the contributor in the event of a conditional approval.

The CI runs should hopefully not be an obstacle in these cases as changes should be contained to localized files/directories which will mitigate the range of detected test cases.
In cases when a maintainer decides nontrivial changes are needed, the maintainer closes or demotes the PR and the contributor is responsible for updating and re-opening or re-requesting review.
1.2: Primary-Maintainer Merge
One common issue that blocks merge is when the primary maintainer of a feature makes a small PR to update an aspect of that feature which they themselves have the most expertise with. In such cases it can be difficult to find a dedicated second reviewer who can confidently approve the changes.
To resolve this I propose we permit core committers to merge their own PRs, provided they follow the validation and isolation requirements of the fast-track specification below.
1.3: Priority Review
I propose that eligible fast-track PRs be automatically labelled as such, and that maintainer review is prioritized towards fast-track PRs. This will involve slack integration, an automated tracking dashboard, and escalation when fast-track-eligible PRs are “stale” for more than N=7 days.
Because fast-track model optimizations are targeted towards a specific model (or small family of models), there should be a small set of assigned reviewers who can be held more directly responsible for triaging fast-track PRs. This burden will be opt-in, but should not be too heavy as triaging fast-track PRs should be very easy by design.
1.4: PR Template
Similar to the PR-Checklist change which updated the PR template, there will be a dedicated template for fast-track PRs which formalizes the requirements and streamlines review. PR will follow the RFC within a few days.
2. Validations and Confidence
2.1: Isolation of Code Changes
The primary risk of merging code tailored to optimize one use-case is impact to other deployments. Performance regressions, breaking other features, or correctness violations are all common side-effects of a seemingly harmless change.
The first pillar of raising confidence in safety is isolation: limiting code changes to a specific deployment scenario.
I propose the initial prototype require that fast-track changes be limited to “flat model” subdirectories (e.g. all diff is within a folder such as vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia).
2.2: Bounded Impact on Deployments

2.1: Isolation of Code Changes
The primary risk of merging code tailored to optimize one use-case is impact to other deployments. Performance regressions, breaking other features, or correctness violations are all common side-effects of a seemingly harmless change.
The first pillar of raising confidence in safety is isolation: limiting code changes to a specific deployment scenario.
I propose the initial prototype require that fast-track changes be limited to “flat model” subdirectories (e.g. all diff is within a folder such as vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia).
2.2: Bounded Impact on Deployments
Optionally, changes can be further gated programmatically (e.g. a kernel fusion only enabled at small input sizes). The more isolated a change is, the smaller the potential impact. By placing rigid bounds on the changes, we can limit the impact to a very small set of deployment scenarios which can be tested explicitly.
Naturally, limiting the scope in this way also reduces the net improvement per PR: other excluded scenarios might benefit from the changes as well. This may also increase code duplication and redundancy. However, it creates a clear path toward improving stability and scalability as we accelerate the pace of optimizations with coding agents.
TensorRT-LLM has merged a design which isolates/replicates model code for each model, hardware, and parallelism triple (e.g. gpt-oss TP1 on SM103). This is a fairly extreme flavor of replication, but it highlights an architectural direction we can move towards for if the initial results from vLLM’s flat-model design prove sufficiently maintainable.
2.3: Explicit Validation of Affected Deployments
Once an isolated and bounded deployment is established for a contribution, what remains is to run sufficient validations against a representative set of configurations.
Since reviewers are still involved in the process, there is some flexibility in the extent of validation: some changes might warrant testing every parallelism configuration or testing on multiple hardwares, while others might be sufficient with only a single parallelism/HW configuration. If a contribution is not sufficiently validated, reviewers may request additional validation and approve conditionally (see 1.1) or they may demote the PR from the fast-track and/or close it as necessary. Submissions following the fast-track accept a higher evidence standard and a higher risk of reviewers closing low-quality PRs wholesale without discussion.
To codify expectations, I propose the following requirements:

E2E Correctness Evaluation:

GSM8k and GPQA-Diamond be run for all proposed model optimizations
A long-context benchmark such as MRCR v2 256K (8-needle) and/or a long-generation benchmark such as AIME25/AIME26 (pass@1 avg1) should be included when changes affect sensitive token-mixing operations such as FMHA or SSM.
A “hard” correctness benchmark such as AIME25/AIME26 (pass@1 avg4+) or HLE or TerminalBench (any) should be included when changes include a “high correctness risk factor”: low-level CUDA C++ or PTX/SASS or equivalent, or new communications kernels for which race conditions cannot be ruled out by formal verification.
All correctness evaluations should use at least “high” reasoning effort, where supported. All evaluations should compare against a known “good” baseline, either referencing official vendor reported numbers or those from a vLLM reference run. Running your own baseline on the vLLM main branch to compare against is acceptable. Measured scores should exceed or match the reference within one percentage point (absolute delta, after accounting for run-to-run variance).
Correctness validation runs should ensure that the deployment scenario is reproduced. For example, if adding a small-batch fusion, GSM8k should run at a correspondingly low batch size (to trigger the change and contribute coverage to the diff).


Kernel Correctness Evaluation:

New kernels should be exhaustively validated for correctness on a broad range of inputs. This includes multiple possible input shapes as well as input distributions.

If bit-exactness is not maintained, it should be justified and validated with a strict tolerance.
If quantization or lossy optimizations are used, this is considered a “high correctness risk factor” and warrants additional E2E validation (see above).


For low-level CUDA kernels, include compute-sanitizer tests such as memcheck, racecheck, and synccheck sanitization are required where applicable.
Note, committed tests should be a small subset of validation performed during development. These should exist strictly for regression checks, not for comprehensive reproduction. We do not want to run exhaustive correctness testing in CI every time we make a model change.


Performance Evaluation:

For low-level CUDA kernels, include compute-sanitizer tests such as memcheck, racecheck, and synccheck sanitization are required where applicable.
Note, committed tests should be a small subset of validation performed during development. These should exist strictly for regression checks, not for comprehensive reproduction. We do not want to run exhaustive correctness testing in CI every time we make a model change.


Performance Evaluation:

PRs should include a “headline” speedup on a specified “target” workload. This is required but not sufficient for performance validation.
Performance change should also be swept across the range of bounded-affected-workloads: multiple concurrencies should be benchmarked almost always, as well as high/low sequence length when applicable. Any throughput or latency regression exceeding 1% for any measured configuration is unacceptable and disqualifies the PR from the fast-track.

For MoE models, ensure real prompts (such as speed-bench throughput_8k) are used so that expert balance is realistic.





Feedback Period.
Feedback period will continue for 12 days, ending on Oct 13. @benchislett will request maintainer review and open a candidate PR with a reference implementation of the proposed design.
CC List.
@njhill @LucasWilkinson @yewentao256 @WoosukKwon @mgoin @vllm-project/vllm-committers @xinli-sw
Discussion Areas

Do we want to further solidify the requirements from sec. 2.3 into a structured requirement matrix? Or do we want to leave it flexible for reviewers to decide on a per-PR basis if validation is sufficient?
How strict should we be about isolating code changes? Are minor one-liner integration patches in core files acceptable, or do we require rigid file-structure-based guarantees about isolation? Can we build static linting tooling (possibly AI powered) that can enforce or verify that changes are limited to the claimed workloads?
Is committer self-merge a good idea, or is it too permissive?
How much control are we comfortable delegating to automated verification systems, versus committer judgement? Should we be more/less aggressive in automating merge workflows?

A new AITER kernel needs an AITER release and the AITER_BRANCH bump in docker/Dockerfile.rocm_base, which already go in their own PR, such as #59794. The model PR then often adds a wrapper in vllm/_aiter_ops.py.
Several open PRs, such as #60397 and #60683, add mono decode kernels for different models, and each one carries its own adapted copy of the same FlyDSL helpers. One shared copy would sit outside every model folder.

Can the tests, the CI step and the wrapper be part of the fast-track PR when they serve only that model folder? Also, should shared code like the mono decode helpers go in a normal PR first?

Details
Root cause. #57652 added AttentionSpec.max_tp_shards and set it to 1 in MLAAttention.get_kv_cache_spec. vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/mla.py (used for the K3 target on NVIDIA and for the DSpark draft on both vendors) builds its own MLAAttentionSpec and leaves it None. On ROCm the K3 target uses MLAAttention (1) while the draft uses this class (None), so MLAAttentionSpec.merge’s per-field AttentionSpec equality check rejects them. _get_kv_cache_groups_uniform_page_size then sees buckets of 69 KDA / 24 target MLA / 5 draft MLA layers instead of 69 / 29, the group size drops from 29 to 5, and the group count goes from 4 (3 KDA + 1 MLA) to 20 (14 + 5 + 1). The server log shows kv cache group sizes growing from 4 to 20 entries and Add 1 padding layers twice instead of Add 18 padding layers.
Why 20 groups is slower. _build_attention_metadata builds per KV cache group each step, and neither the ROCm K3 KDA builder nor the AITER MLA builder supports update_block_table reuse, so every extra group is a full builder.build() plus its own block-table/slot-mapping work.
Why 1 is correct. The draft’s MLA latent KV has a single head and is replicated across TP ranks, same as MLAAttention. On NVIDIA the target and draft both go from None to 1, so they still merge and grouping does not change. kv_tp_replicas remains 1 for K3 because its KDA (Mamba) layers contribute 1 to the gcd, so offloading behavior is unchanged.
Not duplicate. No open PR sets max_tp_shards on the K3 draft spec. #57942 (draft) adds a separate AMD DSpark MLA module, and #58207 changes the group-size heuristic. Both are broader and neither fixes this mismatch on main. This PR is the minimal fix for the regression.

#59853 [Model] Drop the 4x M-RoPE cache headroom for Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8
vllm-project/vllm#59853 · lesj0610 · MERGED · created 2026-10-03T05:32:09Z · merged 2026-10-10T06:51:53Z

Overview
Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 build their M-RoPE cos/sin cache at 4x max_position_embeddings. That headroom exists for Qwen2.5-VL video positions, which these models do not produce, so this sizes the cache like plain RoPE unless video pruning is on.
Claims

4x smaller cos/sin cache per GPU at the default 262k context: 256 → 64 MiB for Qwen3-VL (rotary dim 128), 128 → 32 MiB for Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 (rotary dim 64), and 512 → 128 MiB for Qwen3.5 with YaRN at 1M.
Lower peak while building it, by the same 4x (table below).
No output change without YaRN, since the new cache is a bit-exact prefix of the old one.
With YaRN, Qwen3.5’s correction range now uses the original context length, matching Transformers (#58870).

Validation
Measured on SM80 with each model’s rope parameters:

Validation
Measured on SM80 with each model’s rope parameters:

The 262k cache equals the first 262,144 rows of the old one in bf16 and fp32 (torch.equal). Against ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS["yarn"] on a Qwen3_5TextConfig, 9 of 32 YaRN inverse frequencies differed before and none differ after.
End to end against main, Qwen3.5-0.8B (max_model_len=8192) gives identical prompt logprobs on a 266-token text and identical greedy outputs for text and image prompts without YaRN, and the KV cache gains 15 blocks (60 with YaRN). With YaRN the outputs change, and on that prompt both main and this branch stay at the bf16 noise level against Transformers (mean |Δ logprob| 0.028 and 0.029; 0.025 without YaRN). Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B cut to two layers, on dummy weights in language-model-only mode, give identical greedy tokens and logprobs with the cache at 262,144 rows. With video_pruning_rate=0.5 the cache keeps 1,048,576 rows. Qwen3.8 Flash-Next was not run end to end; its QSA indexer reads the cache at token positions and at the first position of each compressed group, so both stay in range. tests/kernels/core/test_mrope.py and tests/kernels/core/test_rotary_embedding.py pass.

Cache size check

Cache size check

from vllm.config import VllmConfig, set_current_vllm_config
from vllm.model_executor.layers.rotary_embedding import get_rope
 
p = {
  'mrope_interleaved': True,
  'mrope_section': [11, 11, 10],
  'rope_type': 'default',
  'rope_theta': 1e7,
  'partial_rotary_factor': 0.25,
}
with set_current_vllm_config(VllmConfig()):
  for factor in (4, 1):
    rope = get_rope(
      256, 262144, rope_parameters=p, mrope_positions_factor=factor
    )
    print(
      factor, tuple(rope.cos_sin_cache.shape)
    )  # (1048576, 64), (262144, 64)

Details
The 4x came in with Qwen2.5-VL, where temporal positions scale with video duration and can pass the token count. These models use Qwen3-VL’s positions instead: a frame is a (1, h, w) grid spanning max(h, w) positions over h * w tokens, and text advances by one, so the largest position stays below the token count. Qwen3.8-27B runs as Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration; Qwen3.8 Flash-Next inherits the same positions.
MRotaryEmbedding takes the headroom as positions_factor, which defaults to 4. A factor of 1 is passed where each model builds its attention: Qwen3_5DecoderLayer, Qwen3-VL’s text model (Qwen3LLMModel and Qwen3VLMoeDecoderLayer), and Qwen3.8’s QSA attention. Other users of the shared Qwen3, Qwen3-MoE and Qwen3-Next attention keep the 4x, including Qwen3-Omni, whose positions scale with video seconds.
Video pruning keeps the positions of the tokens it drops, so with pruning on the cache stays at 4x. Drafters follow the target’s pruning setting, because some MTP drafters are built from a draft model config that does not carry it. Since pruning now changes the cache shape, ModelConfig.compute_hash includes whether it is enabled.
#58879 fixes the YaRN correction range for every M-RoPE model and leaves the cache size alone. The two overlap only on Qwen3.5 with YaRN and video pruning disabled, where they give the same frequencies.

#59945 [Bugfix][Qwen4Exp] Derive the QSA head_dim from the unsharded head count
vllm-project/vllm#59945 · lesj0610 · MERGED · created 2026-10-04T12:22:40Z · merged 2026-10-07T12:24:41Z

Overview
Qwen4Exp QSA computes its fallback head_dim from num_heads, which is already divided by the tensor-parallel size, so on TP > 1 the fallback is tp_size times too large. The fallback is latent: Qwen4ExpTextConfig defaults head_dim to 256 and rejects None, so only an explicit head_dim: 0 reaches it. This fixes the arithmetic so it matches the hidden_size // total_num_heads idiom used elsewhere.
Claims

The fallback divides by the unsharded head count, so it is correct on any TP size.
No change for any config with a nonzero head_dim, which covers every real checkpoint.

Validation

pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/

Unchanged against main on compute capability 8.0: this is reached only when config.head_dim is 0, which no Qwen3.8-Flash-Next config sets, so no existing test exercises the fallback.
The defect is by inspection of the surrounding lines:

self.total_num_heads = int(config.num_attention_heads)
...
self.num_heads = self.total_num_heads // tp_size
...
self.head_dim = int(config.head_dim or self.hidden_size // self.num_heads)
hidden_size is sized against the unsharded head count, so dividing by the sharded one overstates head_dim by exactly tp_size. q_size and kv_size are then built from it, so the QKV projection is created at the wrong width and the checkpoint fails to load with a shape mismatch rather than producing wrong output.
No test added: the fallback has no checkpoint behind it in the suite, and a test would have to fabricate a config with head_dim: 0 purely to assert one arithmetic expression. The failure mode is a loud shape mismatch, not a silent wrong result.
Not validated end to end: no real checkpoint reaches the fallback.
Details
The same expression appears on the CUDA and ROCm QSA owners and both are changed. total_num_heads is assigned a few lines above the fallback in each, so no reordering is needed.

#59990 [Bugfix] Fix Qwen4Exp PLE embedding rejecting INC (AutoRound) checkpoints
vllm-project/vllm#59990 · vadiklyutiy · MERGED · created 2026-10-05T00:06:48Z · merged 2026-10-05T01:52:08Z
Overview
Fixes #59798. Intel/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AutoRound is an AutoRound checkpoint, which vLLM loads as INCConfig. It failed at model construction with NotImplementedError: Qwen4Exp PLE embedding does not support quantization config INCConfig. Qwen4ExpPLEEmbeddingMethod.from_quant_config now asks INCConfig whether the PLE layer is quantized. #59431 does the same for compressed-tensors.
Claims

The command from the issue (TP=2, expert parallel) no longer raises. Both workers build the PLE n-gram table with Qwen4ExpPLEUnquantizedEmbeddingMethod (bf16), and model construction finishes.
The checkpoint’s own INC metadata makes the choice: its extra_config has ".*ple.*": {"bits": 16, "data_type": "float"}. If INC says the PLE layer is quantized, the old NotImplementedError is still raised, because there is no INC-quantized PLE format.
The branch is in vllm/models/qwen4_exp/common/ngram_embedding.py, so both the NVIDIA and the AMD Qwen4Exp paths get it.
A new unit test covers both cases.

Validation
Hardware: 2 × NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB. Before: commit 18f8f96025b556071eb627076f94df560fbd3a22. After: this PR on top of that commit.
Reproducer, from the issue. No request is needed, because the crash happens at startup:

Validation
Hardware: 2 × NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB. Before: commit 18f8f96025b556071eb627076f94df560fbd3a22. After: this PR on top of that commit.
Reproducer, from the issue. No request is needed, because the crash happens at startup:

VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 vllm serve Intel/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AutoRound \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel
|        | Runs | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------ | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- | --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Before | 1    | Both workers raise NotImplementedError: Qwen4Exp PLE embedding does not support quantization config INCConfig during model construction, before weight loading. The engine exits with code 1. The vllm/vllm-openai:nightly image at the same commit gives the same error. |     | After | 2   | No NotImplementedError in either run. Both workers build the PLE table, and model construction finishes (about 56 s). |
After the fix, both workers log:

Initialized PLE embedding language_model.model.layers.1.ple.ple_embedding.ngram_embedding: quantization_method=Qwen4ExpPLEUnquantizedEmbeddingMethod, weight_dtype=torch.bfloat16, weight_device=cpu, pinned=True

Limitation: neither “after” run reached a ready server. Both runs next stopped at the weight download, with a PermissionError from huggingface_hub. The HF cache on the test machine had only the config and tokenizer files for this model, and we could not write to it. This happens after the bug site, in code the patch does not touch. The “before” run never got that far. No run here loaded the real weights, and no accuracy eval was run. Before merge, someone with the weights should run the reproducer to a ready server and run an accuracy check.
Extra checks (not the reproducer):

The same command with --load-format dummy: weights loaded (35.44 GiB per GPU), CUDA graphs were captured, and the server became ready. One /v1/completions request returned 16 tokens. The text is noise, because the weights are random.
The checkpoint’s safetensors headers on the Hub: the PLE n-gram table is 128 plain BF16 shards ([2500012, 160] each), with no qweight, scales or qzeros. This matches the unquantized method.
Unit tests: pytest --noconftest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py -k "inc_layer_config or rejects_unsupported or modelopt_exclusion or shard_exclusions or mixed_precision" gives 6 passed, 69 deselected. --noconftest was used because tests/conftest.py needs tblib, which the test env did not have. With the INC branch turned off in a separate process (tree unchanged), the new test’s config gets the old NotImplementedError again. So the test catches the bug.
pre-commit run --files on the two changed files: every hook passed or was skipped, including ruff and mypy.

Details
Root cause: from_quant_config gets the model-level quantization config. That config describes the model body, which is not always the same as the PLE table. The method could only ask four config families whether the PLE layer is excluded: ModelOpt mixed precision, ModelOpt, compressed-tensors and FP8. Any other config fell through to the NotImplementedError. This checkpoint quantizes model.language_model.layers to 4 bits, but its extra_config marks .*ple.* as 16-bit float. INCConfig keeps this metadata and resolves it with config_parser.resolve(layer, prefix), but the PLE code never asked it.
How it was found: on the unpatched tree, a debug print just before the raise showed three things. The config was a plain INCConfig, with no handled class in its MRO. The prefix was language_model.model.layers.1.ple.ple_embedding.ngram_embedding. And resolve(None, prefix) returned bits=16, quantized=False. So the INC metadata is already mapped to vLLM names and matches the prefix. Only the dispatch ignored it.
Fix: one if in from_quant_config. For an INCConfig, when quant_config.config_parser.resolve(None, prefix).quantized is false, it returns Qwen4ExpPLEUnquantizedEmbeddingMethod. INCConfig.get_quant_method uses the same resolve(...).quantized check for its own layers. Passing None as the layer is safe: _resolve_raw only uses the layer in isinstance(layer, ParallelLMHead) and layer.__class__.__name__, and both work with None. The compressed-tensors branch also passes None. Size: +6 lines in ngram_embedding.py, and +19 lines of test in tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py. That test file already runs in Buildkite (.buildkite/test_areas/models_basic.yaml).
Design choice for review: INC’s own get_quant_method treats every layer that is not linear or MoE as unquantized, whatever resolve says. This patch is stricter. An INC checkpoint that puts the PLE table inside a quantized block, with no 16-bit exclusion, still gets NotImplementedError. The new test checks this case on purpose. Please say if you prefer INC’s looser behavior.

#59997 [Bugfix][KV Connector][NIXL] Transfer the whole PLE short-conv page in disaggregated P/D
vllm-project/vllm#59997 · aijanai · MERGED · created 2026-10-05T01:53:11Z · merged 2026-10-08T19:58:14Z
Purpose
Fixes #59642 (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 0% MTP acceptance in disaggregated P/D serving with NixlConnector).
The NIXL worker folds every KV cache layer that reports the same base address into one region (register_kv_caches, if base_addr in seen_base_addresses). In the block-outer HMA layout every cache group places its first page at byte 0 of the shared allocation, so on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next the PLE short-conv state (Qwen4ExpPLELayer, a tp-replicated MambaSpec, page = channels × (conv_state_len + num_spec_tokens) = 245760 B) lands in the same region as layer-0 GDN, the layer-3 QSA ring and the layer-3 MLA indexer cache, and that region keeps the MLA page length (204800 B). The PLE descriptors built from block_len_per_layer[_ple_region_index] therefore transfer only 204800/245760 bytes of each PLE slot: 8534 of 10240 channels arrive on the decode worker, the rest is whatever the block held before (never zeroed: the block is exempt from zeroing because an async load is expected to overwrite it). With num_speculative_tokens >= 2 the spec-decode short conv reads those stale columns, the layer-1 hidden state becomes NaN, the target logits are NaN and the rejection sampler rejects every draft (the generated tokens are garbage too, not just slow).

This PR records the PLE page length at registration (_ple_block_len) and uses it for the PLE descriptors on both sides of the transfer (_build_mamba_local / _build_mamba_remote), exchanging it through NixlAgentMetadata.ple_block_len (optional, backward compatible) so the existing P/D geometry check still compares PLE pages. Region discovery is unchanged: the PLE keeps sharing its region with the pages it aliases, as test_csa_linear_registration_discovers_shared_regions expects; only the transfer length of its pages changes.
Test Plan

New unit test tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_ple_region.py: a CSA-linear-like config (MLA + GDN + ring + PLE sharing byte 0 of one block-outer tensor, PLE page larger than the MLA page); asserts the PLE descriptors cover the whole PLE page and that the page length is advertised in the handshake metadata. Before the fix the PLE descriptors carry the MLA page length.
tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector_hma.py + test_nixl_desc_geometry.py run inside the serving image (vLLM 109b5363fc) with the patch hot-patched: 307 passed before and after (one HF-download test deselected).
End-to-end on GB200 (vLLM 109b5363fc + this patch hot-patched into the image, Dynamo + NixlConnector, 1P/1D, nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4, MTP k=3, 200 requests of 64/64 tokens): mean acceptance length goes from 1.00 on 20/21 windows (zero accepted drafts) to 2.7–3.5 on every window, no NaN; the same configuration in aggregate mode gives ~2.1–2.4.

Test Result
See above; details and the full investigation (per-request probes of the PLE conv state on prefill and decode, per-column comparison of the transferred slot) are in #59642.

Details
Why the kernels port unchanged. They are plain Triton. Their PDL path is gated on current_platform.is_arch_support_pdl(), which is false on ROCm, so nvidia/ops/ple.py moves to common/ops/ple.py as is, with the NVIDIA imports updated.
AMD model changes:

Qwen4ExpNGramEmbedding: calls ple_ngram_ids instead of building padded buffers with gathers, a shift and a scatter, and drops the max_num_reqs argument. The pinned-host and device embedding lookups that follow are unchanged.
Qwen4ExpPLELayer:

key_proj and value_proj become one replicated MergedColumnParallelLinear named kv_proj (disable_tp=True, as on NVIDIA).
The gate is ple_gate.
The short conv is ple_conv, which replaces the separate decode, prefill and spec F.conv1d branches with NVIDIA’s single dispatch.
qwen4_exp_ple_short_conv stays a splitting op.


Residual: the fused conv also adds the decoder layer’s residual, so Qwen4ExpDecoderLayer now assigns hidden_states = self.ple(...) instead of adding the PLE output itself.
Weight loading:

ple.key_proj and ple.value_proj map onto the two kv_proj shards.
_HC_WEIGHTS_MAPPER becomes _EXTRA_WEIGHTS_MAPPER, since it now also maps PLE weights.
kv_proj is added to packed_modules_mapping, so a quantization exclude list that names the original projections still applies. The Quark MXFP4 checkpoint keeps both in BF16.
The AMD MTP draft runs without PLE, so it only picks up the mapper rename.



Design choice: a custom op around ple_ngram_ids on AMD. Unlike the NVIDIA path, the AMD model runs the n-gram embedding inside torch.compile, where query_start_loc has a dynamic leading dimension. The kernel’s launch grid comes from the request count, which Dynamo would otherwise trace symbolically. So the call goes through a small opaque op, qwen4_exp_amd_ple_ngram_ids. The new compile test covers that path.

Validated on MI355X (gfx950) only, not MI300X/MI325X (gfx942). The kernels contain no architecture-specific code.

#60023 [Bugfix][Qwen4Exp] Honor —kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers in QSA attention
vllm-project/vllm#60023 · stecasta · MERGED · created 2026-10-05T07:24:37Z · merged 2026-10-05T12:13:32Z
Purpose
Qwen4ExpQSAAttention takes its KV cache dtype straight from cache_config.cache_dtype, so
--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers is silently ignored on every Qwen4Exp full-attention layer, the MTP
draft layer included. This resolves the dtype per layer, the same way Attention and MLAAttention
already do (vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/{attention,mla_attention}.py).
Why it matters: with --kv-cache-dtype fp8, FP8 KV in the MTP layer’s own attention lowers draft
acceptance at depth on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Skipping just that layer (--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers 48)
keeps the target KV in FP8 and restores acceptance.
Evidence
DGX Spark (GB10), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4 @ada4da3, MTP with 6 drafts, greedy, 41 prompts,
c=1, one node, with this change applied (measured on a nightly 0cbac6c-based image; the change is the same two lines on current main):



































target KVMTP-layer KVALdecode tok/sfp8fp83.21543.3bf16fp83.17843.7fp8bf16 (--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers 48)3.47348.7bf16bf163.50450.0
With FP8 KV in the MTP layer, conditional acceptance at depth 2 to 6 is 0.66 to 0.72. With BF16 it
is 0.74 to 0.80. Depth 1 is unchanged.
At 32k context (8 prompts of 32,928 tokens, 6 GiB KV), the skip costs 7% of the KV pool
(211,502 to 196,608 tokens at 3 drafts). Converting the whole cache to BF16 costs 29%.

#60064 [Model][DeepSeek-V4.1] Permute mega-attention wq_b / wo_a while loading
vllm-project/vllm#60064 · aoshen02 · MERGED · created 2026-10-05T14:07:43Z · merged 2026-10-06T05:20:10Z

Overview
DeepSeek-V4.1’s FlashMLA mega attention (the SM100 default) permutes wq_b rows and wo_a columns into the kernel’s layout as a post-load step. That step is only correct when it runs before the linear quant hooks. This PR does the permutation in the weight loaders instead, so it no longer depends on post-load order. It is a prerequisite for #57733.
Claims

Fixes the DSv4.1 dummy-load startup crash on SM100 (DP4: IndexError: index 1280 ...; TP4: a size-mismatch RuntimeError).
Fixes reload_weights (layerwise reload) for mega attention. On main the reloaded wq_b / wo_a are written in checkpoint order and _fused_layouts_ready skips the permutation, so accuracy collapses. Layerwise reload replays the loaders recorded at model init, so with this PR the reloaded shards are permuted again.
Real loads are unchanged: after a TP4 cold load, checksums of every parameter and buffer (1605 per rank, after the quant hooks) match main on all 4 ranks.
Removes finalize_loaded_weights, _fused_layouts_ready, finalize_mega_attn_weights and DSpark’s _finalize_attn (+62 / −94).

Validation
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, real weights, vllm serve, GB200, mega attention (FLASHMLA_MEGA_ATTN_DSV41, confirmed in the logs). GSM8K: 1319 questions, 5-shot, greedy. MegaMoE unless noted.

configmainthis PRDP4 / EP4, mega attention0.8920.896TP4 / EP4, mega attention0.9100.911TP4 / EP4, default MoE backend: GSM8K, reload_weights, GSM8K0.897 → 0.0000.906 → 0.898DP4 / EP4 + DSpark k=5: GSM8K, draft acceptance0.892, 51%0.896, 51%DP4 / EP4, --load-format dummystartup crash: IndexError: index 1280 is out of bounds for dimension 0 with size 1280starts, serves a completionTP4 / EP4, --load-format dummystartup crash: RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (327680) must match the size of tensor b (1280)starts, serves a completion
With MegaMoE, reload_weights collapses on both arms for a separate reason: the model-level post-load step (MegaMoE and mHC state) is not rerun after the layerwise reload finishes. #57733 reruns it; with #57733 and this PR, the same TP4 MegaMoE reload measures 0.901 → 0.898, while #57733 without this PR measures 0.900 → 0.002. The DP4 reload is not measurable on any arm: layerwise reload re-materializes the CPU-offloaded Engram table on the GPU and runs out of memory (pre-existing).

Details
Root cause. permute_wq_b_ derives head_dim from weight.shape[0]. After the CuteDSL linear hook, wq_b is transposed to [K, N], so head_dim is wrong and q_fused_permutation indexes out of bounds. The wo_a BMM hook likewise reshapes wo_a to 3D and packs its scales. A real load calls the permutation from inside load_weights, before the hooks, so it works there. A dummy load never calls load_weights. The model-level process_weights_after_loading then runs after the hooks and crashes.
Fix. permute_on_load(param, perm, dim) wraps the parameter’s weight_loader with composed_weight_loader, so each loaded shard is gathered into the fused layout right after it is written. The wrapping happens in DeepseekV4MegaAttnAttention.__init__, for wq_b.weight, wq_b.weight_scale, wo_a.weight and wo_a.weight_scale. Each of these tensors is loaded by a single weight_loader call (no stacked mapping), so the whole local shard is present when the permutation runs. The quant hooks then see already-permuted tensors, exactly as main’s real load does.
The permutations are computed from the module’s own n_local_heads / head_dim instead of tensor shapes. n_local_heads // n_local_groups == WV_GROUP_SIZE is already enforced in __init__.
Not a duplicate. I searched open PRs for mega attention wq_b, DeepSeek-V4.1 dummy load, fused_layout permute, finalize_loaded_weights and V4.1 mega attn. #57977 touches flash_mla_mega_attn.py for MXFP8 activations but does not change the weight permutation.

#60142 [Bugfix] Fix Qwen4Exp FP8 PLE pinned lookup kernel failing to compile below SM89
vllm-project/vllm#60142 · vadiklyutiy · MERGED · created 2026-10-05T23:02:12Z · merged 2026-10-06T01:56:45Z
Overview
Fixes #59868. On GPUs below SM89 (the report uses 4 × RTX 3090), Qwen4Exp with an FP8 E4M3FN PLE table and --engram-config '{"cpu_offload": true}' crashes in profile_run. The crash is a Triton CompilationError from _lookup_ple_embedding_from_pinned_kernel. This PR makes that kernel copy rows as raw bytes, so the FP8 type never enters its signature.
Claims

_lookup_ple_embedding_from_pinned_kernel now compiles and runs on sm_86 with an FP8 E4M3FN table, and it copies FP8 rows bit-exactly.
On an A40, three existing FP8 pinned-lookup tests in tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py failed before this change. They now pass.
BF16 lookups are unchanged: same bits, same speed.
The module still imports when Triton is not installed.

Validation
Hardware: a machine with 4 × NVIDIA A40 (sm_86). The reproducer uses one GPU. Software: vLLM commit 92044241a (0.30.1rc1.dev648+g92044241a), with and without this PR, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1, Python 3.12.12.
Reproducer. The reported path needs a checkpoint with FP8 PLE weights and a global scale. The public Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next checkpoint has BF16 PLE weights and no scale. So the reproducer launches the kernel directly with a small FP8 tensor. Below is the core of the script that ran. The full script only adds prints and a try/except.

from vllm.models.qwen4_exp.common.ngram_embedding import (
  _lookup_ple_embedding_from_pinned_kernel,
)
 
N, D, BLOCK_D = 4, 16, 16
device = torch.device('cuda', 0)
weight = torch.zeros(N, D, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device=device)
ids = torch.tensor([0], dtype=torch.long, device=device)
output = torch.zeros(1, D, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
 
_lookup_ple_embedding_from_pinned_kernel[(ids.numel(),)](
  weight, ids, output, D, 0, N, BLOCK_D=BLOCK_D
)
torch.cuda.synchronize()

CI gap. On NVIDIA, CI does not run the GPU tests in test_ple.py, and no CI runner is below SM89. So CI cannot catch this bug if it comes back. The runs above are the validation. The AMD MI355 job does run test_ple.py, so it covers the new byte copy on AMD.
Details
Root cause. The kernel’s pointer parameters had no annotations, so Triton took their types from the tensors. An FP8 E4M3FN table became a *fp8e4nv parameter. Triton 3.7.1 accepts fp8e4nv only on compute capability 8.9 and higher. It rejects the type while it lowers the signature, before it compiles the body. That is why the error points at 1:0, the def line. On the A40, a kernel with an empty body and one float8_e4m3fn pointer fails the same way. With float8_e5m2 it compiles.
Fix. The kernel does no math on the values. Its only caller, Qwen4ExpPLEPinnedHostEmbedding._lookup, requires the output dtype to match the weight dtype. FP8 scaling happens later, in PyTorch (dequantize). So the kernel is a pure row gather. Both pointers are now annotated tl.pointer_type(tl.uint8). The caller passes row_bytes = embedding_dim * weight.element_size() and sets BLOCK_D = next_power_of_2(row_bytes). This works for FP8 and for BF16. _reduce_etp_embeddings in the same file already moves FP8 rows as raw bytes. The fix has to be in the signature, because the signature is where the error happens. A uint8 pointer cast inside the body would come too late. A .view(torch.uint8) at the call site would fix _lookup, but not a direct launch with an FP8 tensor like the reproducer.
The fix also needs two more changes:

row_id is now int64. Offsets are now in bytes, so for BF16 row_id * row_bytes is twice the old element offset. An int32 product would overflow at half as many rows as before. With embedding_across_dp, it would overflow at DP × max_num_batched_tokens ≥ 419,431 instead of 838,861 (for example, DP8 × 65,536). tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64) is the usual vLLM idiom.
TritonLanguagePlaceholder gets uint8 and pointer_type. Python evaluates parameter annotations at import time, so without these names the module fails to import when Triton is missing. This is the first tl.pointer_type annotation in vllm/. mypy rejects it, so both lines carry # type: ignore[valid-type].

Limitations.

No end-to-end vllm serve run with an FP8 PLE checkpoint (see Reproducer). Only sm_86 was tested, not sm_80.
_engram_lookup_kernel in vllm/models/deepseek_v41/common/engram.py also takes an FP8 E4M3FN table with no annotation, so it may fail the same way below SM89. It was not run. It does math on the values, so this byte-copy fix does not carry over, and it is not part of this PR.
No model evaluation was run. The lookups are bit-exact in the tests above.

Scope

Layers: K1 + K2 on the 30 backbone layers with the standard mHC seam and no compressor or indexer of their own: 3–7, 9–13, 15–19, 21–23, 25–27, 29–31, 33–35, 37–39. The FFN launch on the other 10: layer 0 (embedding-broadcast seam), the Engram layer 1, and the compressor/indexer layers 2, 8, 14 (also Engram), 20, 24, 28, 32, 36.
Steps: decode only, ≤ 48 rows (8 requests × 1 + 5 DSpark drafts), TP2 or TP4, eager or a FULL CUDA graph. K1 + K2 also need causal SWA windows and fp8_ds_mla KV records.
Everything else runs as before: the DSpark draft layers, and prefill, mixed or larger steps. The paths take and return the same tensors at the layer boundary, so they interleave freely.

Layout

vllm/models/deepseek_v41/amd/mono_decode.py   eligibility per layer / per step, vLLM tensors -> kernel inputs
vllm/models/deepseek_v41/amd/mono/
    runner.py     DSV41MonoLayer: scratch, epoch, peer memory, the launches
    layer.py      K1 / K2 and the FFN launch, composed from the stages below
    attention/    attention stages
    stages/       seam.py (mHC seams, attention reduce), moe.py, moe_shape.py, moe_plan.py, router.py, gemv.py, dims.py
    common/       tagged mailbox, device ops, MX helpers, build keys, peer memory

stages/ and common/ are adapted from ROCm/ATOM’s DeepSeek-V4.1 mono decode (MIT License, commit 97359d6). Each adapted file names its origin and keeps AMD’s copyright notice. The changes from ATOM:

Weights are read in place, with no second copy. The attention linears stay vLLM’s row-major MXFP8 (32×32 E8M0 scales). The routed experts stay in AITER’s shuffled MXFP4 layout.
Path selection. The model is not torch.compiled, so the per-step decision is plain Python. It runs when a FULL graph is captured (uniform decode) and on every eager step. PIECEWISE (breakable) captures are always declined, because they are replayed for mixed batches.
wo_b’s reduce on the FFN-launch layers. Their wo_b is built with reduce_results=False, as the sequence-parallel path already does. A decode step hands the partial to the FFN launch; any other step reduces it in the decoder layer with the same tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce. ROCm’s preshuffled-FP8 wo_b path now honors reduce_results as the linear does. This also fixes a bug on main: with sequence parallelism and an FP8-block checkpoint, wo_b was all-reduced and then reduce-scattered.
TP ranks stay in lockstep. Every rank must take the same path at every layer, since the kernels wait on each other’s pushes. The conditions read only metadata that all ranks hold alike.
Failure modes. An explicit opt-in that cannot run raises: a CDNA version outside the kernels’ (get_cdna_version() in CDNA_VERSIONS, CDNA4 / gfx950 today, so a later generation is one entry once ported), TP other than 2 or 4, FlyDSL missing, expert / data parallelism or EPLB, VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE_A4W4_DSV4, a routed-expert backend other than AITER_MXFP4_BF16, or fewer than 256 compute units (a partitioned GPU: every CTA of a launch must stay resident). The MoE and shared-expert tensors are checked for the kernels’ shapes and dtypes at the first step, as the attention ones are. A layer outside the kernels’ scope is logged once.
All-reduces are exact: fp32 sum in rank order, then bf16. At ≤ 48 rows vLLM’s own decode all-reduces are below the INT4 quick-reduce threshold, so the current path runs them exact too.

All-reduces are exact: fp32 sum in rank order, then bf16. At ≤ 48 rows vLLM’s own decode all-reduces are below the INT4 quick-reduce threshold, so the current path runs them exact too.
A scratch per step width. Hand-offs between CTAs are tagged mailbox pairs in a scratch laid out per step width. Each width has its own scratch, allocated at its first (eager) step: 3–16 MB, and at most 8 widths under DSpark. So a word one width polls as a tag only ever holds tags. The MoE’s task counters outlive a width and live in the epoch buffer.
Dependencies: the flydsl wheel, plus two small AITER helpers that path already depends on: aiter.ops.flydsl.kernels.buffer_ops (FlyDSL’s wheel no longer ships it) and UncachedIpcHeap for peer memory.

No open PR targets DeepSeek-V4.1 mono decode. Searched “dsv41 mono”, “DeepSeek V4.1 mono”, “mono decode layer” and “dsv41_mono”.
The sibling mono-decode PRs are for other models: #59705 (MiniMax-M3) and #60216 (GLM-5).
This PR hooks per decoder layer rather than replacing the model forward, because only 30 of DSv4.1’s 40 layers are eligible.

The race: the kernels hand data between CTAs through tagged mailbox pairs, in a scratch laid out per step width. Every width shared one buffer, so a word one width polls as a tag could hold another width’s plain data. In the failing case, 6-row attention partials lay under 48-row tag words. When one equaled the current tag, a poll took a stale value as published. It came from this PR’s adaptation of ATOM’s kernels, not from ATOM. ATOM zeroes every mailbox buffer before each step, which also wipes whatever another width left. This PR replaced those clears with epoch tags, to drop the host step hook and stay graph-safe, but kept the shared scratch. The fix gives each width its own scratch. The stress test is now clean over 100K replays on each of three layers, and kernel time is unchanged (24 points, mean ratio 1.000).

#60446 [Bugfix][Kernel] Remove invalid NC from Kimi-K3 KDA autotune keys
vllm-project/vllm#60446 · warrendeng · MERGED · created 2026-10-07T17:27:00Z · merged 2026-10-09T14:25:42Z
Overview
Both AMD and NVIDIA Kimi-K3 KDA kernels list NC in their autotune keys even though they have no NC argument. Older Triton ignored this unused entry but Triton 3.9 rejects it at import so this PR removes NC from both copies (fixes test-infra #9028).
Claims

AMD and NVIDIA KDA modules import with Triton 3.9, without changing kernel computation or the effective autotune key used by older Triton.

Validation

With torch==2.15.0+cu130 and triton==3.9.0, unchanged main (a8260cbc5c) fails during KDA test collection with ValueError: key contains names that are not kernel arguments: NC. Importing the NVIDIA copy separately fails the same way.
With the fix, both modules import, and VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest --collect-only -q tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py collects 102 tests. Local pre-commit run --all-files passes.
On an AMD MI350 (gfx950), compared Triton-ROCm 3.8.0+git10f6be36 and 3.9.0+gitaad2a60d with the same Torch build, GPU, inputs, and vLLM sources. The unpatched AMD and NVIDIA modules both fail to import on 3.9; both import with this fix. Both versions import on 3.8.
Ran the actual vendored AMD chunk_kda_fwd_intra(safe_gate=True) kernels on MI350. For a synthetic BF16 input (B=1, T=1024, H=HV=12, K=128, chunk size 64), the defined outputs on patched 3.9 were bit-identical to unpatched 3.8. A ragged input with sequence lengths [63, 73] also matched within rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-6

Details
Triton #11602 added validation of autotune key names. NC = ceil(BT / BC) is computed for the launch grid, not passed to the decorated kernel. The KDA test imports the AMD vendored copy first, masking the same bug in the NVIDIA copy.

#60904 [RFC]: A standard for Specialized (MonoKernels) Decodes in vllm/models
vllm-project/vllm#60904 · dllehr-amd · OPEN · created 2026-10-09T18:25:05Z
Motivation.
A Specialized Decode implementation is one where most/all operations in a model’s forward pass are manually implemented in a way that optimizes for the model’s specific shapes and execution patterns on certain hardware. Typically, these include heavy kernel fusions and overlap for low-latency execution, and custom kernels that tune exact grid sizes for certain batch sizes. These implementations can reach tens of thousands of lines of code, and present a major challenge in managing their complexity. This RFC proposes a standard way to modularize and integrate these runtimes into vLLM under vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/.
Why Specialized Decodes like MonoKernels?
At low concurrency, decode is bound by launch overhead and weight reads, and a MonoKernel removes most of both. On 8× MI350X a graph-mode GLM-5.2 decode step issues ~2,459 kernels in vLLM. With the MonoKernel it issues ~210: 75 MonoKernel launches plus ~135 for dense layers 0–2, input prep and the head.

Proposed Change.
Goals

Opt-in: off by default, enabled with one switch (additional_config={"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"} today).
Refuse at startup: an unsupported deployment fails with one error listing every reason, never a silent fallback.
The model owns it: code lives under vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/specialized_decode/, with no core changes.
One plan() per step: it picks the specialized kernels or vLLM’s stock forward; prefill and mixed batches always run stock.
One step() or run() per pass If specialized_decode exists, run the step() or run() function, else call stock
Fixed batch sizes: the decode kernel declares the batch sizes it serves; larger batches run stock.
Avoid duplicating weights where prudent, reading vLLM’s loaded weights and caches in place.

vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/
    model.py                 # calls specialized_decode_config() in __init__, plan() in forward
    model_state.py           # MRV2 ModelState: builds the decode after load, binds KV caches
    specialized_decode/
        README.md            # supported checkpoints, refusals, options
        runtime/
            __init__.py      # DecodeConfig, batch sizes, specialized_decode_config(), unsupported()
            decode.py        # SpecializedDecode: plan(), run() or Step.layer()
            ...              # weight views, guards, model-specific helpers
        mono/                # the kernels, when the decode uses monokernels
tests/models/<model>/        # proposed: CPU tests for refusals and plan() routing

Instantiation of specialized decode happens at startup

self.specialized_decode_config = specialized_decode_config(vllm_config)
self.specialized_decode = SpecializedDecode(
            self.model, self.specialized_decode_config
        )

Two methods to Available.
Replace the whole forward function with the specialized decode (and let it decide when to call the stock version)

# Kimi-K3 (step mode, #61867): the whole step runs in the specialized decode
decode = self.specialized_decode
step = decode.plan(positions, intermediate_tensors)
if step is not None:
  return decode.run(step, input_ids, inputs_embeds)
return self.model(input_ids, positions, intermediate_tensors, inputs_embeds)
Replace the Decode Layer within the forward function with the specific kernel to run, and let the forward function decide.

# GLM-5.2 (layer mode, #60889): a kernel per layer, or vLLM's layer
step = None if decode is None else decode.plan(positions, intermediate_tensors)
...
kernel = step.layer(idx) if step is not None else None
hidden_states, residual = (kernel or layer)(positions, hidden_states, residual)
Not in Scope

Prefill and mixed steps. These always run vLLM’s layers.
Models compiled with @support_torch_compile.
Launches that span more than two layer (some fusions may fuse end of one layer with beginning of another)
No Runtime fallback. If a megakernel fails the engine should stop.

Enabling and refusal

Prefill and mixed steps. These always run vLLM’s layers.
Models compiled with @support_torch_compile.
Launches that span more than two layer (some fusions may fuse end of one layer with beginning of another)
No Runtime fallback. If a megakernel fails the engine should stop.

Enabling and refusal

Switch: --monokernel (with --no-monokernel), the same for every model and off by default, like --async-scheduling. It sets KernelConfig.monokernel, so it also works from a config file or the Python API.

Additionally we can use --additional_config={"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"} As this will be used in the more generic case.
It applies to the loaded model’s spec. A model has at most one spec per vendor, so there is no name to pick.
There are no other user knobs. Tuning lives in the spec’s options.


Refusal happens in three stages: config (before load), model (after load) and caches (at every bind). Each stage reports every reason, not only the first. If the switch is on and the config is refused, startup raises.
Default-deny: any feature in use that supports doesn’t list is refused, then the spec’s own checks run. The features are: PP, DP, EP, EPLB, DCP, PCP, LoRA, KV connectors, routed-expert capture, speculative decoding, sleep mode, CPU weight offload, weight updates, partitioned GPUs, and EAGLE3 aux layers among the kernel layers.
MonoKernels run only under Model Runner V2.

Things we learned that matter for the standard:

vLLM’s dummy weights make logprob comparisons meaningless. All tensors come from a single seed, so logits are near uniform. The first test drafts showed it: Kimi-K3’s off-vs-off KL (6.7e-3) was the same as its on-vs-off KL (5.7e-3). Each test now uses a realistic random init and asserts the off arm’s entropy and top-1 margin. One trap: seeding by parameter name gives every TP rank the same lm_head shard, so every logit appears TP times and every top-1 margin is exactly 0.
Teacher forcing alone isn’t enough to remove scheduling noise. On MiniMax-M3, off-vs-off KL reached 0.043 until the harness held the scheduler until every request was added. With the hold, its p99 is 1.2e-5, the same as with the engine in process.
Routing moves are expected, not ties. On DSv4.1’s random stack, 13-26 of 256 positions change their routed experts between any two runs. These aren’t ties within the router’s rounding; the top-k margins are just small. The test recomputes routing in float64 from each arm’s MoE input, excludes exactly the moved positions, and caps how many may move.
It has blind spots. On random weights, attention contributes about 1% of the residual. RoPE off-by-one, wo_b scale errors and single-block E8M0 corruption therefore sit at or below the bounds, and Kimi-K3’s routed experts must be damped to keep the stack from going chaotic, which hides them. So this tier sits between the per-stage float64 I/O tests (blocking) and the real-checkpoint E2E. It does not replace the I/O tests.

#61024 [Roadmap] vLLM Roadmap Q4 2026
vllm-project/vllm#61024 · simon-mo · OPEN · created 2026-10-10T19:21:47Z
In #32455, we broke down vLLM’s goals into various special interest groups (SIGs). Building on the Q3 roadmap, please find below each SIG’s Q4 roadmap. You can find regular meetings of these SIGs on the public vLLM calendar.
Key takeaway

Agentic Workload: Q3 established Model Runner V2 as the default and brought production-ready Rust frontend and distributed KV offloading support. Q4 focuses on making optimized agentic serving easier to deploy: better day-0 performance, tuned production recipes, adaptive speculative decoding, richer agent hints, and fault tolerance across hardware.
Ecosystem: We are expanding low-precision serving and checkpoint conversion across NVIDIA and AMD, strengthening speculative decoding and RL integration, and advancing Agentic API and vLLM-Omni. Frontier models and new hardware need a clear path from initial support to validated, optimized production configurations.
OSS Maintenance: We are simplifying engine and model interfaces, completing quantization dispatch refactors, and improving CI coverage, time to signal, security, and performance evaluation. Agent-assisted review and better test-quality checks should help the community maintain a growing model, feature, and hardware matrix.

SIG Core (Meeting Notes)

 Fully remove Model Runner V1 and close the remaining Model Runner V2 gaps.
 Implement extensible KV cache support, pluggable KVCacheConfigBuilder implementations for models, and better cache-grouping heuristics for sliding-window attention speculators.
 Refactor CUDA graphs: separate prefill/decode graph sizes; clarify capture, dispatch, and padding semantics, including adaptive verification and sequence parallelism; and simplify encoder and DeepSeek V4.1 prefill-skipping graphs. Validate prefill graph sizing against padding overhead and performance regressions.
 Simplify and harden the engine’s model loop, data-parallel flow, and scheduler, and improve streaming-input reliability.
 Reduce coupling between model implementations and the engine through a clearer model interface.
 Advance the Rust frontend toward default use, including resolving Responses API readiness and parity requirements.
 Add native per-step observability through forward-pass metrics, in collaboration with Dynamo.


Aspirational work:

Aspirational work:

Simplify KV connector interfaces through standardized KV layouts, including exploring parallel interfaces.
Revisit automatic prefix caching and investigate lookahead EAGLE block caching as a replacement for block dropping.
Explore a more comprehensive scheduler redesign beyond the immediate cleanup.



SIG Large Scale Serving (Meeting Notes)

 Extend agent hints across routers and KV connectors with Dynamo and llm-d: multi-tenancy, cache-tier TTLs, filesystem eviction, and request-level control of prefetching, eviction, and selective offloading.

Lossless state-tree representation for weights and KV cache (~12 bits per value, bit-exact BF16)
Motivation.
LLM decoding is memory-bound: every new token re-reads all the weights and the whole KV cache. Today the way to read fewer bytes in vLLM is quantization, which changes the model’s numerics.
We have been working on state trees Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions⁠ (Ali & Lefkimmiatis, 2026) , a representation in which every value is a path of shared discrete decisions. Its simplest instance shares one exponent node per 64 BF16 values: every weight and every cached key/value is stored in about 12 bits and decodes to its exact BF16 bits, with no calibration and no accuracy trade-off.
We implemented it as an out-of-tree vLLM plugin with fused CUDA kernels github.com/ammarali32/StateTree-Representation:

Weights: a LinearMethodBase for all linear layers, with fused decode-and-multiply kernels for decode and medium batches, and decode + cuBLAS for large prefill.
KV cache: a custom attention backend that stores each 16-token block as a state-tree page, with a decode-attention kernel that reads the compressed pages directly.

The reported bit-exact round trip is useful, but a 16-token compressed page is also written incrementally during decode. Knowledge distillation trains a student model on a teacher’s outputs. A smaller student can reduce the computation needed at inference (Hinton et al., 2015).
Distillation is a training method; the student’s architecture determines which parameters run. Matching the teacher’s outputs gives no evidence that the teacher’s parameters were unused.
conceptually
For one input with N classes, let v_i be teacher logits and z_i student logits. Apply softmax at the same temperature T > 0:
p_i = \frac{e^{v_i/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{v_j/T}},
\qquad
q_i = \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{z_j/T}}. \tag{1}
For example, targets (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and (0.6, 0.1, 0.3) share a top class. Keeping only that label discards which alternative the teacher considers more plausible.
With the teacher fixed, minimize cross-entropy on these soft targets:
C_T = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i \log q_i,
\qquad
\frac{\partial C_T}{\partial z_i} = \frac{q_i - p_i}{T}. \tag{2}
Higher temperatures soften the distributions. The gradient shrinks approximately as T^{-2} in the high-temperature limit.1 With a known class label y, combine this loss with ordinary supervised training:
\mathcal{L}
= \alpha T^2 C_T + (1-\alpha)(-\log q_y^{(1)}),
\qquad 0 \leq \alpha \leq 1,
where q_y^{(1)} uses temperature 1. The T^2 factor keeps the soft-target gradient’s scale roughly stable when changing T (Hinton et al., 2015).
generated responses
R1 distillation used supervised fine-tuning of Qwen and Llama models on 800{,}000 curated examples. Those students learned from response sequences. The report describes no reinforcement-learning stage for the released distill variants (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025, sect. 2.4).

A latent space is the space in which a model’s unobserved variables or internal representations take values. Its coordinates acquire meaning through the model and its training objective.
An autoencoder gives a concrete example. The encoder maps an input x to a code z=f(x). The decoder maps that code to a reconstruction \hat{x}=g(z). Training can minimize mean squared reconstruction error over N examples:
\mathcal{L}(f,g)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert x_i-g(f(x_i))\right\rVert_2^2.
A smaller code can force the model to discard information. What survives depends on which reconstruction errors the loss penalizes, the data, and the capacity of the encoder and decoder. The code can also have as many coordinates as the input, or more. A code with more coordinates is overcomplete. These autoencoders need additional constraints if they are to learn something beyond copying. Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville discuss these cases.
“Similar inputs end up close together” needs a definition of similarity and a distance measure. Reconstruction alone leaves considerable freedom. Suppose a code has two coordinates. Rescale the first coordinate and compensate inside the decoder:
\tilde{f}(x)=\bigl(100f_1(x),f_2(x)\bigr),
\qquad
\tilde{g}(a,b)=g(a/100,b).
The reconstructed inputs are identical because \tilde{g}(\tilde{f}(x))=g(f(x)). Ordinary Euclidean distances between codes have changed: a difference along the first coordinate now contributes 10^4 times as much to squared distance. The reconstruction objective cannot distinguish these two arrangements.
This matters when inspecting a cluster or interpolating between codes. A useful neighborhood has to be established for the task and metric being used. Low dimensionality alone gives no assurance that a straight path through the codes will decode into plausible inputs, or that changing one coordinate will isolate one feature.

Linear maps preserve the algebra of vector spaces: addition and scalar multiplication. They are the core abstraction behind matrices, change of basis, projections, and differentiation (the derivative at a point is a linear map).



definition 



Let V,W be vector spaces over the same field \mathbb F.
A map T:V\to W is linear if for all x,y\in V and a,b\in\mathbb F,
T(ax+by)=a\,T(x)+b\,T(y).
Equivalently, T(0)=0 and T\big(\sum_i a_i x_i\big)=\sum_i a_i T(x_i).


Basic examples



Example 




Identity: I(x)=x; Zero map: 0(x)=0.
Coordinate projections P_i:\mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F, and block projections P_S: \mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F^{|S|}.
Differentiation on polynomials D:\mathbb F[t]\to\mathbb F[t], D(\sum a_k t^k)=\sum k a_k t^{k-1}.
Matrix action: for A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}, T(x)=Ax is linear from \mathbb F^n to \mathbb F^m.



Kernel, image, rank
The kernel and image are subspaces:
\ker T\coloneqq\{x\in V: T(x)=0\},\qquad
\operatorname{im} T\coloneqq\{T(x):x\in V\}.



Theorem 1. Rank–Nullity Theorem (finite dimension) 



If \dim V<\infty, then
\dim V

= \underbrace{\dim \ker T}_{\text{nullity}(T)}

+ \underbrace{\dim\operatorname{im} T}_{\operatorname{rank}(T)}.
In particular, T is injective iff \ker T=\{0\}; T is surjective iff \operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim W.

Theorem 1. Rank–Nullity Theorem (finite dimension) 



If \dim V<\infty, then
\dim V

= \underbrace{\dim \ker T}_{\text{nullity}(T)}

+ \underbrace{\dim\operatorname{im} T}_{\operatorname{rank}(T)}.
In particular, T is injective iff \ker T=\{0\}; T is surjective iff \operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim W.


Matrix representation and change of basis
Fix ordered bases \mathcal B=(v_1,\dots,v_n) of V and \mathcal C=(w_1,\dots,w_m) of W.
There exists a unique matrix [T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in\mathbb F^{m\times n} such that for all x\in V,
\big[ T(x) \big]_{\mathcal C}
 = [T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C} \,[x]_{\mathcal B}.
If \mathcal B'\!,\mathcal C' are new bases with change-of-basis matrices P (domain) and Q (codomain), then
[T]_{\mathcal B'}^{\mathcal C'} = Q^{-1}\,[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\,P.
For endomorphisms (T:V\to V), this specializes to similarity: [T]_{\mathcal B'}=S^{-1}[T]_{\mathcal B}S.



Composition 



For S:U\to V and T:V\to W, [T\circ S]=[T]\,[S] (with compatible bases), matching matrix multiplication.


Invertibility
For T:V\to W with \dim V=\dim W=n<\infty, the following are equivalent:

T is bijective (has a linear inverse T^{-1}).
[T] is an invertible n\times n matrix; \det[T]\ne0.
\ker T=\{0\} and \operatorname{im}T=W.

Operator norm and Lipschitzness
Assume norms \|\cdot\|_V on V and \|\cdot\|_W on W (see norm). The operator norm of T is
\|T\|\;\coloneqq\;\sup_{x\ne0} \frac{\|T x\|_W}{\|x\|_V}

= \sup_{\|x\|_V=1} \|Tx\|_W.

Submultiplicativity: \|T\circ S\|\le\|T\|\,\|S\|.
For matrices with vector p-norms, the induced matrix norms satisfy
\|Ax\|_q\le\|A\|_{q\leftarrow p}\,\|x\|_p.
Special cases: \|A\|_1=\max_j\sum_i |a_{ij}| (max column sum),
\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j |a_{ij}| (max row sum), and
\|A\|_2 equals the largest singular value (see Singular Value Decomposition).




Proposition 1. Linear maps are Lipschitz (finite dimension) 



If \dim V,\dim W<\infty, then every linear T:V\to W is globally Lipschitz:
\|T x - T y\|_W \le L\,\|x-y\|_V\quad \text{for all }x,y,\;\text{with }L=\|T\|<\infty.
Hence linear maps are continuous. This follows because all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent, so \|T\| is finite for any choice of norms.

Hence linear maps are continuous. This follows because all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent, so \|T\| is finite for any choice of norms.





Boundedness vs continuity (general normed spaces) 



For linear maps between normed spaces, “bounded” \iff “continuous” \iff “Lipschitz with some constant”. In infinite dimensions not every linear map is bounded, but in linear algebra (finite dimension) this pathology does not occur.


Computing a Lipschitz constant
Given a matrix A representing T and chosen vector norms, any induced matrix norm provides a Lipschitz constant: L=\|A\|. For the Euclidean norm, L is the largest singular value of A.
Projections and idempotents
A linear map P:V\to V is a projection onto a subspace S along a complement S' if P^2=P, \operatorname{im}P=S, and \ker P=S'. Orthogonal projections require an inner product; see orthogonal projection.
Affine vs linear
An affine map has the form x\mapsto T x + b with T linear and b fixed. Linear maps are precisely the affine maps that fix the origin (b=0).
See also

Vector space — bases, span, and dimension.
norm — norms and induced (operator/matrix) norms.
Inner product space — adjoint, orthogonality, and projections.
Singular Value Decomposition — spectral norm and low-rank structure of linear maps.

strong linguistic relativity says language determines which thoughts a person can have. The evidence supports the weaker claim: language changes which distinctions are cheap to notice or use.
language models let us test the engineering version of the question. We can hold the model and task fixed while changing the prompt language, the language used for intermediate reasoning, or the required output language. A change in output then shows sensitivity to language under that setup. Claims about private thought or human cognition need evidence from another experiment.
what the experiments measure
Ray prompted GPT-4o mini with ten culturally salient questions in thirteen languages, then compared the meanings of its answers with multilingual sentence embeddings. The answers shifted with the prompt language (Pratim Ray, 2025). That gives evidence for language-conditioned output variation in one model on a small prompt set. Distinct minds or conceptual worlds are outside what the experiment measured.
Reasoning models expose another variable because their visible traces can change language before the final answer. Wang et al. tested fifteen languages, seven levels of difficulty, and eighteen subject areas. The tested models often mixed languages, and script had a large effect on when mixing occurred (Wang et al., 2025). Several models routed part of their reasoning through English or Chinese even when the input used another language.
Li et al. studied Chinese and English reasoning in bilingual models. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards increased language mixing, while forcing monolingual decoding reduced accuracy on some mathematical tasks (Li et al., 2025). This is evidence about a learned computation strategy. The human term “code switching” names a similar visible pattern. The cause still has to be shown inside the model.
shared and language-specific representations
Multilingual models contain both shared representations and language-specific routing. Tang et al. identified neurons whose activation predicts the output language. Changing those neurons can steer which language the model generates. Other work finds increasing overlap among representations of equivalent content during multilingual training.
These results can coexist. Sharing a representation saves model capacity when several languages express the same relation. The model still needs language-specific vocabulary, grammar, and output control. A shared concept therefore does not imply identical processing, and a language-specific neuron does not imply a separate concept.
this is the wrong scoreboard for Whorf against universal grammar. Chomsky’s universal grammar is a theory about the human language faculty. It did not predict that neural language models would converge on a specific internal representation. Model compression and transfer results therefore leave that theory and linguistic determinism unresolved.

culture and performance
Prompt language is entangled with the text used for training. English has more data for many tasks, and the English data comes from particular institutions and populations. A model may therefore change its answer because of data volume, translation quality, cultural associations, or the reasoning route it learned. Calling every change “linguistic relativity” hides these causes.
Tao et al. compared model answers with responses from the World Values Survey and European Values Study. The tested GPT models tended to match English-speaking and Protestant European countries more closely. Country identity prompts often moved answers toward the target country’s survey distribution (Tao et al., 2024). The intervention changed an answer distribution. It did not recover a whole cultural worldview, and some prompts made alignment worse.
The same care applies to performance gaps. A lower score in one language can come from less training data, a weak tokenizer, poor benchmark translation, or a model’s preference for another reasoning language. Tests should vary these factors separately. A useful report states the model version, prompt language, reasoning constraint, output language, and task. An average gap without that setup explains little.
what follows
the stable result is narrower: multilingual models share some abstractions and keep some language-specific routes. Prompt language and reasoning language can change accuracy and output distributions. The size and cause of the change depend on the model and task.
This makes language choice an engineering control. Evaluators should test the languages people will use, inspect whether a model silently changes reasoning language, and avoid treating an English result as the default result. If a system serves several cultures, evaluation also needs locally written prompts and local outcome measures. Translation alone preserves words more reliably than it preserves the task.

I use dilectio for love as a practice: sustained attention, care, and commitment to a particular person. Attraction and attachment can arrive unbidden. The practice begins in how I respond.
This is an account of love I can act on. It leaves room for feeling, history, sex, luck, and biology. It also leaves me responsible for what I do with them.



Summary 



Love is attention that survives contact with another person’s reality.


a working model
Three distinctions stop the concept from turning into mush.

Attraction pulls attention toward someone.
Attachment makes their presence and absence matter to the nervous system.
Love as practice is the repeated work of seeing, caring, repairing, and choosing.

Fisher separates mating into lust, romantic attraction, and attachment. These systems can interact and also come apart. Sternberg uses intimacy, passion, and commitment as a second map. (Fisher, 2002; Sternberg, 1986)
These maps classify parts of a relationship. Each gives me a way to locate a failure. Passion can remain while trust collapses. Attachment can remain after a relationship becomes bad. Commitment can become inert if attention has stopped.
My dating heuristic stays brutally simple:

When I do not know what to do, I ask what an emotionally healthy person would do, then I try that.

The heuristic works because it converts a mood into a next action. The other person still gets a vote on whether that action expresses care.
public criteria
Love has public criteria. I infer it from patterns of conduct, memory, attention, and repair. A person remembers what matters to you. They notice changes. They can say what they think you mean and revise that account when you correct them. They protect your agency when stress makes control tempting.
Wittgenstein’s point about criteria helps here. Criteria let us recognize a practice without reducing the practice to a checklist. (Wittgenstein, 1953)
I trust these observations:

They remain curious after forming a confident interpretation.
They can name a mistake without turning the admission into a demand for comfort.
They change conduct after an apology.
They make room for my projects, friends, and solitude.
They tell me when care has become resentment.
They can leave when staying would require self-erasure.

Staying through difficulty is weak evidence on its own. People also stay because of fear, dependence, coercion, habit, intermittent reinforcement, or a lack of alternatives. Love cannot be inferred from duration.
Behaviorism can explain part of the history that produces attachment habits. Reinforcement, punishment, and extinction are real mechanisms. First-person meaning and the value of a commitment require further evidence.
attention and revision
Murdoch treats attention as moral work. The work happens before a dramatic choice, in what I notice, imagine, dismiss, and allow to correct me. (Murdoch, 1970)
This is harder than being nice. Niceness can run from a script. Attention has to survive surprise.
Gadamer’s hermeneutic circle gives the right rhythm. I approach someone with a partial model. Their words and actions revise the model. The revised whole changes how I understand each part. Then I repeat. (Gadamer, 1960)
Love fails when the model stops updating. “I know you” becomes a claim of ownership. A generous interpretation remains answerable to evidence. It can be charitable and still notice contempt, avoidance, manipulation, or incompatibility.

People change. Understanding has to be renewed with them.

This gives epistemic humility a practical form:

Say what I think I heard.
Let them correct it.
Look for the action implied by the correction.
Check later whether the action helped.
